blocks.content: The Indus Valley Civilization (IVC), also known as the Harappan Civilization, was the earliest urban civilization of the Indian subcontinent. It flourished during the Bronze Age and is renowned for its advanced town planning, efficient drainage system, standardized construction techniques, and highly organized urban life. The civilization developed mainly along the Indus River and its tributaries.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Indus Valley Civilization was an advanced Bronze Age urban civilization known for grid-pattern town planning and sophisticated covered drainage systems.
Harappa was discovered in 1921 by Dayaram Sahni, and Mohenjodaro was discovered in 1922 by R. D. Banerjee.
Harappans were the first people in the world to cultivate cotton and conducted trade with Mesopotamia (known as Meluha).
Distinctive archaeological features include Lothal (dockyard), Mohenjodaro (Great Bath), Dholavira (water management), and Kalibangan (fire altars).
The Harappan script is pictographic, written from right to left, and has not yet been deciphered.

blocks.content: The Indus Valley Civilization was discovered in the early twentieth century during archaeological excavations. Harappa was discovered in 1921 by Dayaram Sahni, while Mohenjodaro was discovered in 1922 by R. D. Banerjee. The discovery was announced by Sir John Marshall, which completely transformed the understanding of ancient Indian history.

items: Geographical Extent

blocks.content: The Indus Valley Civilization covered a vast area, making it one of the largest ancient civilizations of the world. It extended from Manda in Jammu in the north to Daimabad in Maharashtra in the south, Alamgirpur in Uttar Pradesh in the east, and Sutkagendor in Baluchistan in the west.

Town planning was the most striking feature of the Indus Valley Civilization. Cities were built on a grid pattern, with roads intersecting each other at right angles. Each city was divided into two parts: the Citadel and the Lower Town.

The drainage system of the Harappan cities was highly advanced. Drains were built with baked bricks and covered with stone slabs. Every house was connected to the main drainage system, indicating a strong civic sense.
Houses were built using standardized baked bricks, usually in the ratio of 1:2:4. Most houses had bathrooms, wells, and courtyards. Multi-storeyed houses were also common.
Important Buildings
The economy of the Indus Valley Civilization was primarily agrarian, supported by trade and crafts. Agriculture was the main occupation.
Major crops included wheat, barley, peas, sesame, and cotton. The Harappans were the first people in the world to cultivate cotton.
The Harappans were the first people in the world to cultivate cotton.
Trade was conducted through the barter system. Both internal and external trade were practiced. Trade relations existed with Mesopotamia, which was known as Meluha in Mesopotamian texts.
The Harappans were skilled artisans. They produced pottery, seals, sculptures, and jewelry. The famous bronze Dancing Girl and stone statue of the Priest King reflect their artistic excellence.
The religious life of the Harappans is understood through archaeological evidence. They worshipped the Mother Goddess, animals, trees, and a proto-Shiva figure represented by the Pashupati seal.
The Harappan script was pictographic and written from right to left. It has not yet been deciphered.
The exact cause of the decline of the Indus Valley Civilization is unknown. Various theories suggest floods, earthquakes, climatic changes, decline in trade, or external invasions.

The social life of the Harappans can be understood through archaeological remains such as houses, ornaments, toys, burials, and seals. Society appears to have been well- organized and urban in nature.

The Harappans consumed wheat, barley, rice (in some regions), pulses, fruits, and vegetables. Animal products like milk and meat were also part of their diet. Fish was commonly consumed in coastal areas.

People wore cotton and woollen clothes. Ornaments were popular among both men and women. These included necklaces, bangles, earrings, rings, and anklets made of gold, silver, copper, shell, ivory, and semi-precious stones.

items: 1. Games and Entertainment
Games and Entertainment

blocks.content: Various toys such as toy carts, whistles, dice, marbles, and figurines have been found. This indicates that children and adults engaged in recreational activities.

The Harappans used a standardized system of weights and measures. Weights were usually cubical and made of chert. They followed a binary system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, etc.), which reflects advanced commercial practices.

items: Discoveries: Harappa (1921 - Dayaram Sahni) and Mohenjodaro (1922 - R.D. Banerjee) under the announcement of Sir John Marshall.
Key Site Features: Dockyard at Lothal, Great Bath at Mohenjodaro, Granaries at Harappa, Water Management at Dholavira, and Fire Altars at Kalibangan.
Construction & Materials: Standardized brick ratio of 1:2:4 was used, and seals were predominantly made of steatite.
Script & Trade: Script was pictographic, written right to left (undeciphered); trade with Mesopotamia was recorded as trade with Meluha.

blocks.content: Burial practices indicate religious beliefs. Three types of burials have been identified: complete burial, fractional burial, and symbolic burial. Bodies were generally buried in north-south direction.

No clear evidence of kings or palaces has been found. This suggests that the Indus Valley Civilization may have been governed by a decentralized or collective authority, possibly by merchants or priests.

Seals were an important feature of the Harappan Civilization. Most seals were made of steatite and depicted animals such as unicorn, bull, elephant, rhinoceros, and tiger. Seals were used for trade, identification, and religious purposes.

Pottery was generally red with black designs. The Harappans were expert bead-makers, producing beads from carnelian, lapis lazuli, agate, jasper, and shell. Bead-making centres included Chanhudaro and Lothal.
The Harappans had knowledge of geometry, measurement, metallurgy, and town planning. Their use of standardized bricks and advanced drainage reflects scientific thinking.

Several theories have been proposed regarding the decline of the Indus Valley Civilization. These include repeated floods, earthquakes, climatic changes, drying up of rivers like Saraswati, decline in trade, and invasion theories. However, no single theory fully explains the decline.
